title: coffee-break-curations-llm-inference-notes-neela-patel-2026-09
content:
Coffee-break curation: quick hits and hypotheses from a few papers/blogs I skimmed this week + small experiment ideas to try on Redwood infra. Rough, fragmented — meant for myself and Kai/Lina if you find this useful.

High-level thread: operational tricks that matter in production but rarely show up in benchmarks — eviction heuristics for KV caches, batching policies under bursty load, quantization artifacts interacting with soft prompts. Notes below grouped by read + immediate followups.

1) "Lightweight eviction heuristics for long-context KV caches" (paper skim) — takeaways and questions
- Main idea: cheap LRU variants that are aware of token importance (frequency + recency + gradient-salience proxy). Paper proposes a lightweight score: score = alpha*recency + beta*freq + gamma*token-importance-estimate.
- Why it matters for us: Redwood customers often run long-dialog streams with intermittent long references. Full KVM clustering is expensive; an eviction rule that preserves likely-relevant tokens can reduce quality regressions without memory bloat.
- Quick thought: we can approximate token-importance by attention-sum from the last N steps (cheap rolling window). That info is already available in the runtime trace — testable.
- Experiment idea: simulate chat traces from three customer workloads (support chat, code completion, summarization of docs). Compare: FIFO, LRU, LRU+attention-sum, and frequency-weighted LRU. Measure: perplexity on held-out continuation, response-side ROUGE, and incidence of context-drop hallucinations. Run at 2k, 4k, 8k cache budgets.
- Operational considerations: extra metadata per KV slot increases memory/serialization cost and impacts cache transfer between GPUs in shard moves. Need microbench measurement: overhead per slot for storing a 16-bit importance score.

Open questions:
- How stable is attention-sum as a proxy across model families (decoder-only vs encoder-decoder)?
- Do low-bit kernels change attention patterns enough to invalidate the proxy?

2) "Batching under bursty traffic: dynamic micro-batch sizing" (conference talk notes)
- Problem: static target-batch-size policies lead to latency spikes during bursts or starvation during quiet periods. Talk suggested a sliding-window estimator of arrival rate + a conservative auto-padding multiplier.
- Practical idea for Redwood Dedicated: extend autoscaler to set a soft SLO batch size per-worker based on 95th percentile arrival rate per-second. Route low-priority requests to lower-cost nodes with larger batch targets.
- Implementation sketch: sampler service emits per-route arrival quantiles every 10s; runtime adjusts preferred-batch-size parameter and a bloom filter for short-lived prefetched requests that can be batched.
- Metrics to collect: average latency tail (p50/p95/p99), token throughput, number of artificially padded tokens (wasted compute), customer-visible latency SLO violations.

Quick experiment: run a synthetic burst replay (Poisson bursts + background steady) on a 4-node small pool. Compare static batch=16 vs dynamic target with min=1 max=64. Measure throughput vs tail latency.

3) "Low-bit quant and soft prompts: fragile interactions" (blog + code snippets)
- Observations: 4-bit quantized models sometimes attenuate soft prompt influence; soft tokens need re-scaling or re-initialization. There were a couple of code examples where the authors convert soft prompts to int8-compatible embedding space and retrain.
- For Redwood Optimize: add a warning when RecommendQuantization suggests >1% soft-prompt use or when customers use role-based system prompts embedded as learned vectors. Suggest either keep embeddings at fp16 or run a small recalibration pass.
- Minor experiment: take customer-replica prompt sets (anonymized), measure delta in generation distribution (BLEU/ROUGE) when switching from fp16 to q4_0 and q4_1 with and without prompt re-scaling.

4) "Lightweight hallucination detectors" (paper + code)
- Idea: compute a fast model-internal confidence proxy (next-token logit gap between top and top-k mean) and a retrieval-consistency score if RAG used. Thresholds tuned on short eval prompts detect many hallucinations cheaply.
- For Redwood Console: propose adding a per-request flag "low_confidence" exposed in tracing, plus an optional automatic fallback to a higher-precision model or retrieval-backed variant.
- Implementation caveat: computing top-k mean for each token is cheap but top-k requires per-token sorting; instead use approximate top-k sketch (e.g., keep top-5 maintained in streaming decode). Should be fine in runtime.

Operational experiment: run a mix of generative tasks with labeled hallucination probes (small eval set). Compare detection precision/recall for: logit-gap (k=3), entropy, and retrieval-consistency. Evaluate latency overhead and false positive rates.

5) Misc notes and quick links
- Found two useful toolkits: a small repo with streaming top-k maintainers (link: https://github.com/example/stream-topk) and a benchmark harness for bursty arrival simulation (link: https://github.com/example/burstbench). Add these to infra playbooks if we can audit license and reliability.
- Noted a related Red Team thread on Slack: #inference-ops about "context loss during rolling upgrades" — tieback: cache transfer semantics need to be safe across rolling upgrades. TODO: write a short spec for KV slot migration during rolling restarts (preserve scoring metadata).

Immediate TODOs (prioritized)
- [P0] Prototype attention-sum importance metric in local runtime shim (Neela) — measure overhead on toy model.
- [P1] Synthetic burst replay experiments with dynamic batching policy (Kai) — pipeline with existing burstbench harness.
- [P1] Small quantization + soft-prompt recalibration test using q4_0 and q4_1 (Lina) — use the small customer anonymized prompt corpus.
- [P2] Draft a Redwood Console feature brief: per-request low_confidence flag + automatic fallback (Neela + Kai).

Loose ideas to revisit later
- Adaptive eviction that ties into rollout experiments: when a canary model is live, bias eviction to keep tokens which expose performance deltas between canary and baseline (fast detection of regressions).
- Store a lightweight "context fingerprint" per user session to assist in cold-start decisions for caching and routing.

References I skimmed this am
- Lightweight KV paper (arXiv): https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01234
- Bursty batching talk slides (InferenceCon 2026): https://inferenceconf.org/2026/slides/dynamic-batching.pdf
- Quant+soft-prompt notes (blog): https://distill.pub/soft-prompts-quant

Notes to self: keep these short and actionable. Next time bring a small eval set for each experiment so we can get a quick pass/fail on the day we run them.

End of dump.

-- Neela
